problem: Image-centric implicit memory for lifelong navigation needs hundreds of historical frames in context, but a native Qwen2.5-VL ViT yields ~598 tokens per frame, so cost and attention noise explode and only tens of images fit. Object-centric memories (maps, object queries) depend on upstream detectors and generalize poorly across domains.
motivation: Lifelong navigation requires reusing long visual histories to explore efficiently in new scenes and shorten paths in familiar ones. Raw visual streams are highly redundant, so strong, task-aligned visual token compression should make long implicit memory affordable. The paper is inspired by DeepSeek-OCR's extreme compression.
key_idea: Compress each frame from 598 to ~30 tokens with a frozen DINOv3 encoder plus PixelUnshuffle+Conv blocks feeding the first block of Qwen2.5-VL-3B's ViT, so hundreds of frames fit in one VLM context for end-to-end lifelong navigation.
insight: Moderate compression retains navigation-relevant information while greatly cutting cost: 16x compression on 50 images cuts train time 26.4s→6.5s and memory 90.6→46.8GB with SR 60.2→56.6, whereas 64x collapses SR (42.5 at 50 images). Longer memory is not monotonically better (16x: 100 imgs 57.5 > 200 imgs 55.2), and 4x with 100 images is best (63.2). Category analysis shows DINOv3 helps salient objects (shower glass 53→92) but hurts texture/boundary categories (carpet, island, microwave).
method: Base feature extractor: frozen DINOv3-ViT-Base (patch 16) encodes each 720x640 RGB frame into a 45x40 patch grid (padded to 48x40).

Compression blocks: N=2 blocks, each PixelUnshuffle (2x2 to channels) then stride-1 3x3 Conv + BatchNorm + SiLU; 4^N spatial reduction; last conv projects channels to 1280 to match Qwen ViT hidden size.

Positional encoding and merger: add 2D positional encodings on the 12x10 grid, then a 2x2 patch-merger yields 30 tokens per frame (no CLS/register tokens), fed directly into first block of the Qwen2.5-VL-3B ViT; projector and LM unchanged.
Sequence formulation: input [SYS; (P1,I1);...;(PT,IT); INSTR] with camera poses serialized as text; the model outputs natural language with <coordinate>x,y</coordinate> for a frontier or target.
OVON-500K data: generated following MTU3D over 145 scenes with occupancy-map frontiers; sub-goal frontier chosen by min shortest-path cost with small random exploration.
GOAT-1M data: lifelong multi-goal episodes over 136 scenes with memory lengths 50/100/200/500 steps (GOAT-1M-50L/100L/200L/500L), filtered to avoid too-short trajectories.

setting.training_data: 1.5M samples: OVON-500K + GOAT-1M-50L/100L/200L/500L, generated in HM3D scenes; 32 H20 GPUs, lr 1e-5, up to 2 epochs
setting.observation: egocentric RGB (720x640) history with camera poses as text
setting.action_space: predicted frontier/target 2D coordinates as text (data uses discrete MOVE_FORWARD/TURN_LEFT/TURN_RIGHT/STOP)
setting.privileged: none stated (poses given as input; frontier/occupancy map used for training data generation)

numbers.extra: text says SPL 34.8 while the table prints 34.9

numbers_note: Ablation SRs (uniformly sampled subset of GOAT Val-Unseen) are in tables not listed above: 4x/100 images 63.2, 16x/100 images 57.5, 1x/50 images 60.2. The main GOAT tables use full splits, with val-seen-synonyms being a non-canonical split name.
results: On GOAT-Bench Val-Unseen it reaches 62.7 SR / 56.9 SPL versus the strongest baseline MTU3D's 47.2 / 27.7. On HM3D-OVON Val-Unseen it reaches 62.5 SR / 34.9 SPL versus MTU3D's 40.8 / 12.1. Gains hold on seen and synonym splits.
limitations: Compression gives a small accuracy drop versus uncompressed (60.2→56.6 at 50 images), and very long contexts (200+) degrade rather than help.
Frozen DINOv3 features struggle with texture and boundary-sensitive targets (carpet, island, microwave).
Only simulated HM3D evaluation; the ablations use a uniformly sampled subset of Val-Unseen, and text/table numbers are slightly inconsistent (SPL 34.8 vs 34.9).
